subject: How are CPO and PIT values calculated for sequential data

messages.author: 30d2a095f756b8ef
messages.subject: How are CPO and PIT values calculated for sequential data
parts:
I'm studying the wonderful book by Virgilio for an application to a time series problem I have. 
While going through this chapter

https://becarioprecario.bitbucket.io/inla-gitbook/ch-temporal.html#sec:autotime

and reading on the diagnostics I thought of asking, is there a special treatment of how WAIC, CPO, and PIT values are calculated in this context?

For instance, if CPO are cross-validatory metrics, and provide a probability of y[i] being observed when all by y[i] are used, should we not consider the probability of observing y[i] when only y[1:n-1] are observed?

Thank you for the amazing work and my apologies if this has been answered before.
Best wishes,
Jesus

messages.author: 334c7505e0b5cf65
messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] How are CPO and PIT values calculated for sequential data
parts: Hi,
> and reading on the diagnostics I thought of asking, is there a special treatment of how WAIC, CPO, and PIT values are calculated in this context?
I do not think that there is any special case for time series implemented in INLA.

>
> For instance, if CPO are cross-validatory metrics, and provide a probability of y[i] being observed when all by y[i] are used, should we not consider the probability of observing y[i] when only y[1:n-1] are observed?

I think that what you mean is some ‘predictive’ metrics using past observations only, right? Although I can see why this is useful for time series, I think that you would be looking at a different metric than CPO. However, this does not mean that your proposal is not useful, but that they are two different things.

Best,

Virgilio

messages.author: afb003e064114795
messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] How are CPO and PIT values calculated for sequential data
parts: On Mon, 24 Aug 2020 at 13:19, Virgilio Gómez-Rubio <becario...@gmail.com> wrote:

> For instance, if CPO are cross-validatory metrics, and provide a probability of y[i] being observed when all by y[i] are used, should we not consider the probability of observing y[i] when only y[1:n-1] are observed?

I think that what you mean is some ‘predictive’ metrics using past observations only, right? Although I can see why this is useful for time series, I think that you would be looking at a different metric than CPO. However, this does not mean that your proposal is not useful, but that they are two different things.

log-CPO is essentially the log-predictive likelihood score, but under leave-one out prediction, and can be computed relatively efficiently because of the small perturbation to the model caused by leaving just one observation out.
Computing the predictive scores for leave-future-out prediction is much more expensive, especially if the hyperparameter distributions should also depend only on the past data.
For the hybrid score of using the full posterior for the hyperparameters, one option is to use the "config" output from inla and compute the time-series predictive distributions "manually" as a post-processing step.

Finn
 

Best,

Virgilio

parts:
You'd need to go through the maths for you particular model (e.g. if it has non-Gaussian observations you may need some approximations) but the principle works the same as that used in other hidden-Markov time series models; the Cholesky factor already encodes the predictions, when computed for the time series ordered nodes.
I haven't done this in an inla context, so I'm not sure how difficult it is to work out the details.

Finn

messages.author: afb003e064114795
messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] How are CPO and PIT values calculated for sequential data
parts:
I'm not sure what you mean by cpo for m predictions, but yes, you can do "brute force" predictive calculations like this:

Method 1:
Fit model to first 1:n observations, and extract cpo for the n:th observation.
Repeat that for all n.

That would give you full one-step-prediction scores.

If you're ok with using a joint point estimate of the parameters, this is an option:
Method2:
Estimate the full joint model using all data
Do method 1, but with hyperparameters fixed to the joint estimate (the theta-mode or the theta-mean)

A hybrid method is to integrate over the joint hyperparameter posterior:
Method3:
Estimate the full joint model using all data
For each hyperparameter configuration in the "config" output,
  do method 1, but with hyperparameters fixed to one configuration at a time

The log-predictive score for observation n is then

\log p(y_n|y_old) \approx \log \sum_k p(y_n|y_old, theta_k) p(theta_k|y_all)

where p(y_n|y_old, theta_k) is the one-step-prediction density for observation n (as in Method 1)
for a fixed hyperparameter configuration theta_k,
and p(theta_k|y_all) is the posterior density for (the integration weight given in the "config").

Finn

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] How are CPO and PIT values calculated for sequential data
parts:
If the use case you have in mind is an "online estimation" setting, where the model parameters are updated as more data comes in, then method 1 is appropriate, but if the use case is to estimate a model off-line, and then apply it to a sequence of data with forward prediction, then Method 2 is more appropriate.

Finn
